questions.question: Why use background jobs in a Rails app?
questions.title: Why Background Jobs
questions.direct_answer: Background jobs move slow work out of the request cycle so the user gets a fast response. Sending an email (SMTP can take seconds), generating a PDF, calling a slow API, importing a CSV — if done in the controller, the user waits and the request can time out. Instead, enqueue a job (MailJob.perform_later(user), returns in ~1ms) and a worker does the slow work later. Benefits: fast responses (happy users), reliability (jobs retry on failure — a network blip doesn't lose the email), scalability (workers scale independently of web), and scheduling (send the email at 9am tomorrow). The cost: a queue store (Redis), job infrastructure, and the need for idempotency. Rule of thumb: if work takes >100ms or calls an external service, push it to a job. Sidekiq is the common backend.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know background jobs move slow work out of the request so the user gets a fast response, with retry/scale/scheduling.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Doing slow work (email, PDF, external API) in the controller — user waits, request may time out.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Background jobs move slow work out of the request (email, PDF, API, CSV). Fast response, retry, scale, schedule. >100ms or external -> job.

sections.title: Why background jobs
sections.content:
```ruby
# WITHOUT a background job: slow work in the controller -> user waits
def create
  @user = User.create!(user_params)
  Mailer.welcome(@user).deliver_now    # SMTP can take SECONDS
  PdfReport.generate(@user)          # slow
  ExternalApi.sync(@user)            # may time out
  redirect_to @user                    # user waited the whole time
end

# WITH a background job: enqueue, respond fast
def create
  @user = User.create!(user_params)
  MailJob.perform_later(@user.id)      # ~1ms (returns immediately)
  PdfJob.perform_later(@user.id)
  SyncJob.perform_later(@user.id)
  redirect_to @user                    # fast response; worker does the rest
end

# The worker does the slow work LATER (and retries on failure):
class MailJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(user_id)
    user = User.find(user_id)
    Mailer.welcome(user).deliver_now   # slow, but off the request
  end
end

# Benefits:
#   - fast responses (user doesn't wait for email/PDF/API)
#   - reliability (jobs retry on failure; a blip doesn't lose the email)
#   - scalability (workers scale independently of web dynos)
#   - scheduling (MailJob.set(wait_until: 9am).perform_later)
# Cost: Redis (queue store), job infra, idempotency.

# Rule of thumb: >100ms OR external service -> push to a job.
```
